about: Physics blocks whose maths is a formula (ND3b): each keeps its id, ports and results, and its maths is the Equation below, with a name that says what happens.

references: Murray, C. D. and Dermott, S. F. 1999, Solar System Dynamics, Cambridge University Press. doi:10.1017/CBO9781139174817

source.text: Murray, C. D. and Dermott, S. F. 1999, Solar System Dynamics, Cambridge University Press

explain.curious: In a pair, both bodies pull on each other, so the orbit depends on their combined mass.
explain.science: The two-body problem reduces to one body moving under the total mass G(M + m).

references: Murray, C. D. and Dermott, S. F. 1999, Solar System Dynamics, Cambridge University Press. doi:10.1017/CBO9781139174817

equation.name: Length of a year
equation.formula: P = 2 * pi * sqrt(a * a * a / (G * M))

source.text: Murray, C. D. and Dermott, S. F. 1999, Solar System Dynamics, Cambridge University Press

explain.curious: The farther out a world orbits, the longer its year, and not just in proportion: four times farther means eight times longer.
explain.science: Kepler's third law for two point masses, using the sum of both masses. Exact for an isolated pair; other bodies perturb it slightly.

references: Murray, C. D. and Dermott, S. F. 1999, Solar System Dynamics, Cambridge University Press. doi:10.1017/CBO9781139174817

equation.name: Size of the orbit from the length of a year
equation.formula: a = cbrt(G * M * P * P / (4 * pi * pi))

source.text: Murray, C. D. and Dermott, S. F. 1999, Solar System Dynamics, Cambridge University Press

explain.curious: Knowing how long a year lasts and how heavy the star is tells you how far away the world must be.
explain.science: Kepler's third law solved for the semi-major axis. Used when a catalogue gives a period but not a distance.

references: Murray, C. D. and Dermott, S. F. 1999, Solar System Dynamics, Cambridge University Press. doi:10.1017/CBO9781139174817

equation.name: Closest and farthest points of the orbit

source.text: Murray, C. D. and Dermott, S. F. 1999, Solar System Dynamics, Cambridge University Press

explain.curious: An oval orbit has a closest and a farthest point; the more stretched it is, the bigger the difference.
explain.science: Geometry of the ellipse: periapsis a(1 - e), apoapsis a(1 + e).

references: Murray, C. D. and Dermott, S. F. 1999, Solar System Dynamics, Cambridge University Press. doi:10.1017/CBO9781139174817
Hamilton, D. P. and Burns, J. A. 1992, Icarus 96, 43 (periapsis form) https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1992Icar...96...43H

equation.name: Reach of a world's own gravity

r.name: radius of the bubble its gravity rules

source.text: Hamilton, D. P. and Burns, J. A. 1992, Icarus 96, 43

explain.curious: Around every world is a bubble where its own gravity beats its star's. Moons have to live well inside it.
explain.science: Hill sphere radius at periapsis, for a body much lighter than its host. Prograde moons are long-term stable out to roughly a third to a half of it.

params.description: 2.44 for a fluid satellite, 1.26 for a rigid one

references: Murray, C. D. and Dermott, S. F. 1999, Solar System Dynamics, Cambridge University Press. doi:10.1017/CBO9781139174817
Chandrasekhar, S. 1969, Ellipsoidal Figures of Equilibrium, Yale University Press (fluid coefficient)

equation.name: Closest a moon can come before tides tear it apart

k.name: how the moon holds together (fluid 2.44, rigid 1.26)

source.text: Murray, C. D. and Dermott, S. F. 1999, Solar System Dynamics, Cambridge University Press

explain.curious: Get too close to a big world and its tides pull a moon apart. That is where rings live.
explain.science: Roche limit for a satellite held together only by its own gravity. A fluid body breaks up at about 2.44 primary radii for equal densities, a rigid one at about 1.26.

references: Eggleton, P. P. 1983, Approximations to the radii of Roche lobes, ApJ 268, 368: r_L/a = 0.49 q^(2/3) / (0.6 q^(2/3) + ln(1 + q^(1/3))), good to 1 % for any mass ratio. doi:10.1086/160960

equation.name: How big a star can swell before its partner's pull takes its gas

q.name: this star's mass over its partner's

rL.name: radius of the sphere with the same volume as the star's Roche lobe

explain.curious: Each star in a pair owns a teardrop of space. A star that swells past the tip of its teardrop starts spilling gas onto its partner.
explain.science: Eggleton's fit to the volume-equivalent radius of the Roche lobe, good to about 1 % for all mass ratios. Used for every pair the generator makes. Unverified until the paper search returns.

params.description: mass above which the rate stops growing, solar masses (5)

references: Hurley, J. R., Tout, C. A. and Pols, O. R. 2002, Evolution of binary stars and the effect of tides on binary populations, MNRAS 329, 897: overflow rate F(M) [ln(R/R_L)]³ M☉/yr with F = 3e-6 (min(M, 5))² (eq. 58), capped by the donor's thermal timescale τ_KH = 1.5e7 M (M − M_c) / (R L) yr in solar units (eq. 61). https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0201220

equation.name: How fast gas pours off a star that overfills its lobe
equation.formula:
mc = min(M / M_sun, Mcap)
over = ln(max(x, 1))
mdot = f * mc * mc * over * over * over * M_sun / yr

M.name: mass of the star giving gas

x.name: star's radius over its Roche lobe's

f.name: rate at one solar mass, solar masses a year

Mcap.name: mass above which the rate stops growing, solar masses

mdot.name: mass leaving the star through its inner point

source.text: Hurley, J. R., Tout, C. A. and Pols, O. R. 2002, MNRAS 329, 897

explain.curious: The further a star bulges past its teardrop, the faster its gas pours across to its partner.
explain.science: The rule-of-thumb rate from the binary evolution code BSE, steep in the overfill so the star settles just at its lobe; capped elsewhere by how fast the star can adjust (its thermal timescale). Unverified until the paper search returns.
